name: Array literal
desc: Creates a new array from the values between the brackets, in order.

name: Array.from()
desc: Builds a real array from any iterable or array-like value, with an optional mapping function.
body: The source can be a string, a `Set`, a `Map`, another array, a `NodeList`, or any object with a `length` property. The second argument receives the value and the index, so a fill loop becomes one call. `Array.from` copies, so the new array and the source do not share elements changed later at the top level.

name: Array.of()
desc: Creates an array with exactly the arguments as elements, including a single number.
body: `new Array(7)` treats a single numeric argument as a length and creates seven holes. `Array.of` treats every argument as an element, so `Array.of(7)` has length one. Use `Array.of` when the value comes from a variable and might be a number.

name: length
desc: Reads the number of slots, which is one more than the highest index. Assigning it truncates or extends the array.
example:
// Data shape: list of city names
const cities = ['Vienna', 'Graz', 'Linz'];

console.log(cities.length);              // 3
console.log(cities[cities.length - 1]);  // 'Linz'

cities[6] = 'Salzburg';   // writes past the end
console.log(cities.length); // 7, indexes 3 to 5 are holes

cities.length = 2;        // truncates, 'Linz' and the rest are gone
console.log(cities);      // ['Vienna', 'Graz']
body: `length` is not the count of values when the array has holes. Setting it smaller deletes every element at or above the new length, and setting it larger adds empty slots. Both are silent, so a wrong assignment can destroy data without an error.

name: at()
desc: Reads one element by index and accepts negative numbers to count from the end.
body: Bracket access with a negative number does not read from the end; it looks up a property named `-1` and returns `undefined`. `at` is the method form that handles the offset. On a string it returns a character the same way.

name: push()
desc: Adds values at the end and returns the new length.
body: `push` mutates the array and returns the new length, not the array. Chaining `push` therefore gives you a number, not something you can push again. For a new array instead of a mutation, use `[...guests, 'Csilla']`.

name: pop()
desc: Removes the last element and returns it. Returns undefined when the array is empty.
body: `pop` and `push` together make a stack: last in, first out. Both work at the end of the array, so neither moves the other elements and both stay fast on large lists.

name: shift()
desc: Removes the first element and returns it, moving every remaining element one place left.
body: Every call moves the remaining elements to a lower index, which costs time proportional to the length. Draining a list of ten thousand items with `shift` is much slower than walking it with a `for` loop. Use `shift` on short lists or keep an index pointer for long ones.

name: unshift()
desc: Adds values at the front and returns the new length. Every existing element moves up.
body: The values keep their argument order, so `unshift('a', 'b')` puts `a` before `b`. Like `shift`, it moves the whole array, so it is the expensive end. If the list is only read from the front, `push` plus a reverse at the end is cheaper.

name: splice()
desc: Removes elements from a position, optionally inserts new ones, and returns the removed elements.
body: The start position, the number to delete, then the values to insert. Omitting `deleteCount` deletes to the end, so `splice(0)` empties the array and returns everything. The method mutates the original and returns a new array of removed elements. Keep it apart from `slice`, which copies and mutates nothing.

name: slice()
desc: Returns a shallow copy from start up to but not including end. The original is unchanged.
body: `slice()` with no arguments is the shortest way to copy an array. The copy is shallow, so objects inside are shared with the original. `slice` never mutates its input, which is the opposite of `splice` in both name and behaviour.

name: concat()
desc: Returns a new array with the elements of the original followed by the elements of each argument.
body: `concat` flattens one level of array arguments. Non-array arguments are appended as single elements. It always returns a new array, so chaining it is safe.

name: join()
desc: Builds one string from all elements, placing the separator between them.
body: The default separator is a comma, so `join()` and `join(',')` give the same result. `null` and `undefined` elements become empty strings rather than the words. `join` is the usual last step of a `map` chain that prints output.

name: includes()
desc: Returns true when the array contains the value, comparing with SameValueZero.
body: Use `includes` for primitives and for a yes or no answer. For an array of objects, the value must be the same reference, so a freshly built object never matches. Use `some` with a predicate in that case.

name: indexOf()
desc: Returns the index of the first strict match, or -1 when nothing matches.
body: `indexOf` uses strict equality, so it never finds `NaN` and never matches two objects with equal contents. Always test against `-1` before using the result as an index. `lastIndexOf` searches from the end.

name: find()
desc: Returns the first element for which the callback returns true, or undefined.
body: The callback gets the element, the index, and the array. `find` stops at the first true, so put the most likely match first only if that ordering is meaningful; otherwise it is just an early exit. `findIndex` returns the position instead of the element.

name: findIndex()
desc: Returns the index of the first element that passes the test, or -1.
body: `findIndex` is the object-aware version of `indexOf`: it takes a test instead of a value. The `-1` result must be checked before using it in `splice`, because `splice(-1, 1)` removes the last element rather than doing nothing.

name: filter()
desc: Returns a new array with the elements for which the callback returns true.
body: The result is always a new array, possibly empty, never `undefined`. The callback should be a pure test; pushing into an outside array from inside `filter` defeats the point and makes the result confusing. Combine with `map` for the common keep then reshape chain.

name: map()
desc: Returns a new array with one output per input, in the same order.
body: `map` keeps the length. Elements where the callback returns `undefined` stay in the result as `undefined`, so filter first if the output must be dense. Use `map` for the value it returns; use `forEach` when the point is a side effect.

name: reduce()
desc: Folds the array into one value by carrying an accumulator from element to element.
body: The callback receives the accumulator, the current element, the index, and the array, and must return the next accumulator. Without the starting value, `reduce` uses the first element as the seed and begins at index 1, and throws `TypeError` on an empty array. Pass a starting value for sums, counts, grouping and any case where the array can be empty.

name: some()
desc: Returns true when at least one element passes the test, and stops at the first pass.
body: `some` answers whether a match exists without building an array. It short circuits, so callbacks with side effects run only until the first true. On an empty array it returns `false`.

name: every()
desc: Returns true only when every element passes the test, and stops at the first failure.
body: `every` on an empty array returns `true`, which follows from the definition: there is no element that fails. That surprises people validating input, so check `length > 0` as well when an empty list is not acceptable. The counterpart `some` returns `false` on an empty array.

name: sort()
desc: Sorts in place. With no comparator it compares elements as strings, which is wrong for numbers.
body: The comparator returns a negative number when `a` comes first, positive when `b` comes first, zero for a tie. `a - b` sorts numbers ascending. Since ES2019 the sort is stable, so equal elements keep their input order. `sort` mutates, so copy with `[...list]` or use `toSorted` when the original order must survive.

name: forEach()
desc: Runs a function once per element for its side effects and returns undefined.
body: `forEach` cannot `break`, and returning from the callback only skips the current element. Use `for...of` when you need `break`, and `map`, `filter` or `reduce` when you need a value. Changing the array inside the callback shifts the remaining indexes and skips elements.

name: flatMap()
desc: Maps each element and flattens the results one level into a single array.
body: `flatMap` is `map` followed by `flat(1)` in one pass. It is the shortest way to turn a list of parents into a flat list of children. Return a non-array and it is appended as a single element.
